facts.text: Pan's Labyrinth (2006, dir. Guillermo del Toro) won three Academy Awards at the 79th Academy Awards: Best Art Direction (Eugenio Caballero, Pilar Revuelta), Best Cinematography (Guillermo Navarro) and Best Makeup (David Martí, Montse Ribé).
Pan's Labyrinth also won three BAFTA Awards, including Best Film Not in the English Language, plus the Hugo Award for Best Dramatic Presentation, Long Form; it grossed about $83 million worldwide.

Pan's Labyrinth (Mexico, Spanish-language) was also nominated at the 79th Academy Awards for Best Foreign Language Film, Best Original Screenplay (del Toro) and Best Original Score (Javier Navarrete), but won only its three technical awards.

Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street (2007, dir. Tim Burton) won the Golden Globe for Best Motion Picture - Musical or Comedy and Johnny Depp won the Golden Globe for Best Actor - Musical or Comedy at the 65th Golden Globes.
Sweeney Todd received three Oscar nominations at the 80th Academy Awards (Best Actor for Johnny Depp, Costume Design, Art Direction) and won Best Art Direction.

Let the Right One In (2008, Sweden, dir. Tomas Alfredson) won four Guldbagge Awards (including Best Director, Best Cinematography and Best Screenplay), the Tribeca Founders Award for Best Narrative Feature, the Saturn Award for Best International Film and the Empire Award for Best Horror Film.
Let the Right One In was nominated for Best Film Not in the English Language at the 63rd British Academy Film Awards; an American remake, Let Me In, followed in 2010.

The Others (2001, dir. Alejandro Amenabar) earned 15 nominations at the 16th Goya Awards and won eight, including Best Film, Best Director and Best Original Screenplay - the first English-language film without Spanish dialogue to win Best Film at the Goyas.

The Others won three Saturn Awards at the 28th ceremony (Best Horror Film, Best Actress for Nicole Kidman, Best Supporting Actress for Fionnula Flanagan); Kidman was nominated for a Golden Globe (Best Actress - Drama) and a BAFTA for it.
The Ring (2002) won Best Horror Film and Best Actress (Naomi Watts) at the 29th Saturn Awards.
Saw (2004) was nominated for Best Horror Film at the 31st Saturn Awards.

I Am Legend (2007, dir. Francis Lawrence, starring Will Smith) grossed $585,532,684 worldwide, ranking No. 3 on Wikipedia's list of highest-grossing horror films (behind It (2017) and The Sixth Sense (1999)) - the highest of any 2000s horror release.

I Am Legend opened to $77.2 million in December 2007, the highest December opening weekend at the time, beating The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King, until The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey (2012).

Among 2000s releases on Wikipedia's highest-grossing horror list, M. Night Shyamalan's Signs (2002) grossed $408,250,578 worldwide (No. 11), Hannibal (2001) $351,692,268 (No. 16) and Van Helsing (2004) $300,157,638 (No. 25).

Paranormal Activity (shot for $15,000 by Oren Peli) had a limited US release on September 25, 2009 and a nationwide release on October 16, 2009; it grossed $194,183,034 worldwide and is often cited as the most profitable film ever by return on investment.

Paramount acquired the Paranormal Activity US rights from Peli for $350,000 and shot a new ending costing an additional $200,000; in its first full wide weekend it took No. 1 with $21.1 million from 1,945 theaters, beating Saw VI.
Saw (2004) was made for roughly $1-1.2 million and topped its opening weekend, grossing about $104 million worldwide ($103,911,669 on the list).

The Saw franchise (10 films to date) has grossed $1,141,842,812 worldwide, the fifth-highest-grossing horror franchise; Saw III (2006) is its top earner at $164,874,275, followed by Saw II (2005, $152,925,093) and Saw IV (2007, $139,352,633).
Guinness named Saw 'the most successful horror franchise in history' in 2010.

The Ring (2002) grossed $249.3 million worldwide on a $48 million budget, opening to $15 million on 1,981 screens and becoming a sleeper hit with $129.1 million in the US; its sequel The Ring Two (2005) grossed $163,995,949.

In the Final Destination series, The Final Destination (2009) grossed $187,384,627, Final Destination 3 (2006) $118,890,272, the first film (2000) $112,880,294 and Final Destination 2 (2003) $90,941,129.

The Final Destination (2009) is the highest-grossing film of the original run of the series at $187,384,627; Final Destination 3 (2006) grossed $118,890,272, the first film (2000) $112,880,294 and Final Destination 2 (2003) $90,941,129.

The Resident Evil film series passed $1.2 billion and was once the highest-grossing horror and video-game film series; the original series' six films total $1,237,978,176, led by The Final Chapter ($314,101,190).

Remakes at the box office: The Texas Chainsaw Massacre (2003) opened to $29.1 million and grossed $107.4 million worldwide on a $9.5 million budget; Dawn of the Dead (2004) opened to $27.3 million and grossed $102.3 million; Halloween (2007) grossed $80.4 million on a $15 million budget.

Remakes at the box office: The Texas Chainsaw Massacre (2003) opened to $29.1 million and grossed $107.4 million worldwide on a $9.5 million budget; Dawn of the Dead (2004) opened to $27.3 million and grossed $102.3 million; Halloween (2007) grossed $80.4 million.

The Saw films were released every October in the US: Saw (Oct 29, 2004, dir. James Wan), Saw II (Oct 28, 2005, Darren Lynn Bousman), Saw III (Oct 27, 2006), Saw IV (Oct 26, 2007), Saw V (Oct 24, 2008, David Hackl), Saw VI (Oct 23, 2009, Kevin Greutert).

Saw was created by James Wan and Leigh Whannell, premiered at Sundance on January 19, 2004 before its October 29, 2004 release by Lions Gate, and follows serial killer John 'Jigsaw' Kramer (Tobin Bell).

Final Destination (2000) was based on an unused spec script by Jeffrey Reddick originally written for The X-Files; the 2000s entries are Final Destination (2000), Final Destination 2 (2003), Final Destination 3 (2006) and The Final Destination (2009, dir. David R. Ellis).

The Resident Evil films, based on Capcom's games, star Milla Jovovich as the film-original Alice: Resident Evil (2002, Paul W. S. Anderson), Apocalypse (2004, Alexander Witt) and Extinction (2007, Russell Mulcahy).
Hostel (2005) was written and directed by Eli Roth and executive produced by Quentin Tarantino among others; it follows American tourists in Slovakia.
Underworld (2003, dir. Len Wiseman in his feature debut, starring Kate Beckinsale as Selene) grossed $95.7 million on a $22 million budget and launched a franchise about vampires and lycans.

The Ring (2002, dir. Gore Verbinski, written by Ehren Kruger) is a remake of the 1998 Japanese film Ring, based on Koji Suzuki's 1991 novel, and its success inspired American remakes of other Asian horror films.
The Grudge (2004) was directed by Takashi Shimizu, remaking his own 2002 Japanese film Ju-On: The Grudge; it stars Sarah Michelle Gellar and was produced by Sam Raimi.
Dark Water (2005, dir. Walter Salles, starring Jennifer Connelly) remakes Hideo Nakata's 2002 Japanese film Dark Water, based on Koji Suzuki's short story 'Floating Water'.
Pulse (2006, dir. Jim Sonzero, co-written by Wes Craven, starring Kristen Bell) is an English-language adaptation of Kiyoshi Kurosawa's 2001 Japanese film Pulse.
The Texas Chainsaw Massacre (2003) was directed by Marcus Nispel (feature debut), produced by Michael Bay, and remade Tobe Hooper's 1974 film; Nispel also directed the 2009 Friday the 13th reboot.
Dawn of the Dead (2004) was directed by Zack Snyder in his feature debut from a James Gunn screenplay, remaking George A. Romero's 1978 film, with Sarah Polley and Ving Rhames.
Rob Zombie wrote and directed Halloween (2007), a remake of John Carpenter's 1978 film and the ninth Halloween film, with Malcolm McDowell as Dr. Loomis and Tyler Mane as Michael Myers.

Friday the 13th (2009) is a reboot and the twelfth film in the franchise, with Jared Padalecki and Derek Mears as Jason Voorhees; The Last House on the Left (2009, dir. Dennis Iliadis) remakes Wes Craven's 1972 film and opened to $14.1 million.

James Wan directed Saw (2004) in his feature directorial debut from a script by Leigh Whannell, who also co-starred alongside Cary Elwes; after failing to get the script made in Australia, they shot a short film of the same name to attract producers.
Saw was shot in 18 days on a budget of about $1–1.2 million and went on to gross $104 million worldwide after Lions Gate picked it up following its January 2004 Sundance screening.
Nick Frost made his film debut in Shaun of the Dead (2004), a film inspired by an episode of Edgar Wright and Simon Pegg's sitcom Spaced; Pegg and Wright co-wrote it.
Zack Snyder made his feature directorial debut with the 2004 Dawn of the Dead remake, written by James Gunn, with original-film actors Scott Reiniger, Tom Savini and Ken Foree in cameos.

James Gunn made his directorial debut with the sci-fi horror comedy Slither (2006), starring Nathan Fillion, Elizabeth Banks and Michael Rooker; it grossed about $12 million against a $15 million budget.
Eli Roth made his directorial debut with Cabin Fever (2002), co-written by Roth, which grossed over $30 million against a $1.5 million budget after Lionsgate bought it at TIFF.
T.J. Miller made his film debut in Cloverfield (2008), directed by Matt Reeves and written by Drew Goddard.
Marcus Nispel made his feature directorial debut with The Texas Chainsaw Massacre (2003), the first film produced by Michael Bay's Platinum Dunes, starring Jessica Biel.
Michael Dougherty made his directorial debut with the anthology Trick 'r Treat (2007), produced by Bryan Singer and starring Dylan Baker, Anna Paquin and Brian Cox.
J. A. Bayona made his full-length directorial debut with The Orphanage (2007), produced with help from Guillermo del Toro, who asked to double the film's budget and shooting time.
Alison Lohman starred in Sam Raimi's Drag Me to Hell (2009) after Elliot Page, originally cast as Christine, dropped out over SAG-strike scheduling issues.
Malcolm McDowell was cast as Dr. Loomis in Rob Zombie's Halloween (2007), with Tyler Mane, who had worked with Zombie on The Devil's Rejects, playing the adult Michael Myers.
Neil Marshall cast The Descent (2005) with an all-female ensemble, after his business partner pointed out that horror films rarely have all-female casts.
Final Destination (2000) was directed by James Wong in his directorial debut and began as a spec script by Jeffrey Reddick for an episode of The X-Files; Devon Sawa, Ali Larter and Kerr Smith star.
Paranormal Activity (2007) was shot for $15,000; DreamWorks then bought it and added a new ending costing $200,000, and it grossed about $194 million worldwide.

Paranormal Activity had no real script: Oren Peli gave the actors story outlines to improvise, a 'retroscripting' technique also used on The Blair Witch Project, and he auditioned 'a few hundred people' before choosing Katie Featherston and Micah Sloat.

Cloverfield (2008) had the working titles Slusho, Cheese and Greyshot, was secretly greenlit by Paramount in February 2007, and earned $172.4 million against a $25 million budget; its first teaser ran untitled before Transformers (2007).
Cloverfield producer J. J. Abrams conceived it after seeing Godzilla toys in Japan, wanting 'our own American monster'; the creature was designed by Neville Page.

The Descent (2005) shot its cave interiors on sets built at Pinewood Studios (designed by Simon Bowles) because real caves were too dangerous; it grossed $57.1 million worldwide on a £3.5 million budget.

28 Days Later (2002), directed by Danny Boyle and written by Alex Garland, grossed $82.8 million on an $8 million budget; Westminster Bridge and other busy London spots had to be filmed early in the morning or with streets briefly closed.
Garland said playing the video game Resident Evil (1996) reminded him how much he loved zombies, which led to the 28 Days Later screenplay that Boyle liked after making The Beach (2000).
Wolf Creek (2005) was made for $1.1 million, shot in South Australia almost entirely on high-definition video; writer-director Greg McLean drew on the murders by Ivan Milat and Bradley Murdoch.

Hostel (2005) was made for $4.8 million and grossed $82 million; Eli Roth got the idea from Harry Knowles, who told him about a Thai 'murder vacation' website, and Quentin Tarantino was an executive producer.

The Texas Chainsaw Massacre (2003) grossed $107 million on a $9.5 million budget, and The Ring (2002) grossed $249.3 million worldwide, while Dawn of the Dead (2004) grossed $102.3 million on $26 million.

Drag Me to Hell (2009) was shot in Tarzana, California in 2008 on a $30 million budget as Sam Raimi's return to horror after the Spider-Man trilogy; Raimi cameoed as an uncredited ghost at the séance.
[REC] (2007) by Jaume Balagueró and Paco Plaza was filmed in late 2006 in Barcelona, at a real fire station with real firefighters; it was shot in chronological order.
'I want to play a game.' - Jigsaw, Saw (2004); the same Jigsaw quote list also includes 'Game over!'.
'Seven days.' - Samara Morgan's whispered phone warning after the cursed tape is watched, The Ring (2002), directed by Gore Verbinski.
'You've got red on you.' - a line repeated to Shaun by various characters in Shaun of the Dead (2004); Shaun himself yells 'Come and get it! It's a running buffet!' to distract the zombie horde.
'Rule #1 for surviving Zombieland: Cardio.' - Columbus (Jesse Eisenberg) narrates in Zombieland (2009); Rule #2 is 'The Double Tap'.
'Time to nut up or shut up.' - Tallahassee in Zombieland (2009); Columbus's closing line is 'Cardio, seat belts, and ... a little sunscreen never hurt anybody.'
'Because you were home.' - Dollface's answer when Kristen asks why they were targeted, The Strangers (2008); Pin-Up Girl later says 'It will be easier next time.'
'Hello. I am Princess Moanna, and I am not afraid of you.' - Ofelia to the giant toad in Pan's Labyrinth (2006), directed by Guillermo del Toro.
'That was longer than a heartbeat.' - Jim (Cillian Murphy) to Selena after she tries to kill him in 28 Days Later (2002).

Ju-On: The Grudge (2002) by Takashi Shimizu was the third Ju-On installment and the first theatrical one; Shimizu remade it in English as The Grudge (2004) with Sarah Michelle Gellar, which grossed $187.3 million.
Kiyoshi Kurosawa's Kairo (Pulse, 2001) premiered in Un Certain Regard at Cannes; an English-language remake, Pulse, followed in 2006.
Hideo Nakata's Dark Water (2002), whose original Japanese title echoes Koji Suzuki's anthology From the Depths of Dark Water, was remade in English in 2005 by Walter Salles with Jennifer Connelly.
Kim Jee-woon's A Tale of Two Sisters (2003) is the highest-grossing South Korean horror film and was remade as The Uninvited (2009); it is based on the Joseon-era folktale Janghwa Hongryeon jeon.

Bong Joon-ho's The Host (2006), about a Han River monster, debuted at Cannes' Directors' Fortnight on May 21, 2006, and became South Korea's highest-grossing film of all time; it was inspired by the 2000 McFarland formaldehyde incident.
Park Chan-wook's Thirst (2009), a vampire tale based on Zola's Thérèse Raquin starring Song Kang-ho, won the Jury Prize at the 2009 Cannes Film Festival.
Banjong Pisanthanakun and Parkpoom Wongpoom's Thai ghost film Shutter (2004) was the fifth-highest-grossing film of the year in Thailand.
The Eye (2002) by the Pang brothers was a Hong Kong–Singaporean co-production shot in Hong Kong and Thailand, remade in 2008 with Jessica Alba.

Spain: J. A. Bayona's The Orphanage (2007) opened at Cannes with a standing ovation of over 10 minutes and won seven Goya awards, including New Director.
Spain: Jaume Balagueró and Paco Plaza's [REC] (2007) is set in a quarantined Barcelona apartment block, was remade as Quarantine (2008), and had a sequel, [REC]² (2009).
France: Alexandre Aja's High Tension (2003) was filmed in Romania, screened at TIFF's Midnight Madness, and was released in the UK as Switchblade Romance.
France: Julien Maury and Alexandre Bustillo's Inside (2007), starring Béatrice Dalle and Alysson Paradis, was their directorial debut and was released in France on June 13, 2007.
France: Pascal Laugier's Martyrs (2008) caused walkouts at the Marché du Film in May 2008, and its initial 18+ French rating was cut to 16+ after an appeal.
France: Xavier Gens made his feature debut with Frontier(s) (2007), in which Paris criminals hole up at a neo-Nazi-run inn.
Sweden: Tomas Alfredson's Let the Right One In (2008), adapted by John Ajvide Lindqvist from his novel, was shot in Luleå in 2007 and won four Guldbagge Awards.
Norway: Tommy Wirkola's Dead Snow (2009) pits students against Nazi zombies and was released in Norway on January 9, 2009; Roar Uthaug's slasher Cold Prey came in 2006 and was shot in Jotunheimen.
Japan: Yoshihiro Nishimura's Tokyo Gore Police (2008) stars Eihi Shiina and remakes his 1995 film Anatomia Extinction.
